 You don't need higgs for that, you can also just call API's directly, but since I had access to it, I used it.

content:
In 2026+, this is the way to go:

1) mobile app: KMP, either compose or native ui for both, common logic

2) backend + database: custom on Hetzner VPS (I run Node.js) + Postgres/sqlite database on the same server, with Coolify

3) storage: Cloudflare R2

4) landing page: Vercel + Vercel CLI for easy and fast deployment

5) domains: Cloudflare or Porkbun

6) auth: Firebase Auth (it's free), easy to hook up to your backend

7) notifications: Firebase FCM

8) backup: Hetzner VPS backup + Backblaze + R2 via script on your backend

This makes everything so much faster because Claude/Codex can directly SSH or use API/MCP to connect to those and do the necessary changes

content:
A few months ago, I build 100% this idea. 

It looked the same and behaved in the same way (chat on the side, itinerary/map on the right), even the pre-loaded header with image was placed and looked the same 😂. 

It had a memory about the user, tailored recommendations, and was connected to 3rd party to recommend activities. Almost 100% feature parity.

Not saying to brag, the pattern is pretty common here on what the consumer expects and what features to build.

I've decided to stop the project because it was hard to make it *great*. The results were too generic, and I didn't feel like releasing a sub-par product. 

One of my solutions to tackle this problem was to load recommendations from YT/TikTok videos, which are more up-to-date and more local, less generic.

But then, to load all the assets and data properly, I still needed to use Google Places API/Mapbox or other and those are pricier than some of the top LLM models. 

Which is fine, but that changes the entire payment model and affects growth somewhat, as monetization needs to occur faster to recover costs. 

Getting funding makes sense here, since it's easier to swallow those costs vs being bootstrapped.

The website is still live for but I killed the server so the service doesn't work: http://getfinna.com (I spent too much time rendering the landing page animation btw)

I think the market and the idea are great, so I'm curious about how Francis's startup will evolve.

Nonetheless, the project is working (let's say 80% done) and is for sale. DM.

It had a memory about the user, tailored recommendations, and was connected to 3rd party to recommend activities. Almost 100% feature parity.

Not saying to brag, the pattern is pretty common here on what the consumer expects and what features to build.

I've decided to stop the project because it was hard to make it *great*. The results were too generic, and I didn't feel like releasing a sub-par product. 

One of my solutions to tackle this problem was to load recommendations from YT/TikTok videos, which are more up-to-date and more local, less generic.

But then, to load all the assets and data properly, I still needed to use Google Places API/Mapbox or other and those are pricier than some of the top LLM models. 

Which is fine, but that changes the entire payment model and affects growth somewhat, as monetization needs to occur faster to recover costs. 

Getting funding makes sense here, since it's easier to swallow those costs vs being bootstrapped.

The website is still live for but I killed the server so the service doesn't work: http://getfinna.com (I spent too much time rendering the landing page animation btw)

I think the market and the idea are great, so I'm curious about how Francis's startup will evolve.

Nonetheless, the project is working (let's say 80% done) and is for sale. DM.

content:
I think about this tweet from @PierreDeWulf  often because there is a lot of truth to it, based on my observations.

For example, Cal AI. They've entered the market with already strong validation from top players. I don't remember how much MyFitnessPal was doing, but it was $10M+, which is top tier among the mobile apps. 

And don't get me wrong, the entire team was talented, and they pushed it relentlessly, but they chose a market with a high ceiling from the start. 

I don't think they would be able to grow as big if they chose a less potent market. And I'm not trying to diminish their talent. The team worked hard and did big bets. But in the smaller market, the ceiling would be lower.

Now I'm observing the same about Pokémon TCG apps. Obviously, the scale is different here (compared to calorie tracking), BUT the entire market is growing, which funnels a lot of traffic to the app stores. 

Those who were early and managed to claim top position in the ASO are now benefiting from free traffic that's funneled from all the players that are doing paid UA or social. 

@adamlyttleapps was one of the first with his Pokémon scanner app, and he was very open about the app and its metrics. #buildinpublic brought him a lot of competitors... and most likely also boosted his organic traffic via ASO.

More competitors meant more time and money spent on marketing, which grew the entire pie. In the end, people had to *learn* that it's even possible to scan their card to estimate the value.

And his app was perfectly positioned via ASO to benefit from all the extra traffic that was not branded.

I think that's a good example of building in public that actually benefits one more than it hurts. 

On top of that, obviously, the entire Pokémon brand grew recently, which funneled the growth even further. 

Those who joined later still benefited from the growing pie, but it seems that they have to put more effort into paid UA to compensate for the free traffic from ASO. 

The App Store algorithm is still putting a lot of weight towards the age of the app, especially if those are on top.

So yea, sometimes, choosing the right market or spotting the trend is half of the battle and determines whether you are playing on easy or hard mode. I think.

content:
there is something to it, I had to figure out a lot of stuff just to have some fun

in Poland back then that window was even bigger since we were not getting all the latest tech as fast

one example was figuring out how to set IP connections between PCs just so we can do a LAN party together, tbh I don't even remember how I was able to figure it out 

now it's so easy with dedicated software or LLM's guiding through everything

the other memory I have is when we all wanted to play Counter Strike 1.6 together in my small town

in order to do that, we needed to create our own private network between our PCs and one of us needed to host the game

at that time we found out about Hamachi which enabled us to do just that

the issue was that our internet speed was 0.5Mbit, which meant that we were only able to reliably host 3vs3 without any lags

then I remember one friend who had 1Mbit internet hosted a game, which enabled us to play 5vs5

that was something

it might be just a nostalgy, but there was something fun and unique with all those obstacles that we had to overcome & I think till this day I have this ability to figure the shit out pretty fast

content:
Those posts of Flutter vs RN vs KMP vs native always seem to spark lots of discussions.

Probably because most defend what they work with. 

Now with agents, it's very easy to create a proof of concept in each one of those and compare the results. 

It can be done in less than a day.

That's how I decided on KMP after seeing the results. 

I asked Claude to build a simple app with animations, took 3-4h of prompting/refining, and the results were pretty clear for me.

Kotlin was the winner because of its state management, so the transition between animations looked nice and smooth.

Then there was SwiftUI. The animations were nice, almost on pair, but the transitions were not as smooth.

I tried to do the same with Flutter, but the results were disappointing, and I didn't want to keep pushing it. 

(No I didn't try React Native with Expo)

Now. Maybe it's the framework, or maybe it's Claude being able to work better with Kotlin vs other frameworks.

But even if it's Claude's capability, then it's enough for me to switch because this mf is writing 100% of my code now :)

My bet is that KMP will be growing in popularity (let's see how this ages in few years)

content:
I agree on some of those takes.

I think in some ways it is overhyped and I have friends who are trying to set it up and find a use case for them but they haven't found it yet.

Here are my use cases:

Business:
1) Me and my co-founder have one channel where we run the ads operation. The bot has API access to our ad analytics and helps us pull the data and make decisions.

2) Inspo/bookmarks page: we just drop links to our bot and he analyzes and categorizes them in one database and displays on the website.

3) Bug reports page: whenever there is some bug for me to patch, we drop it via chat and he adds it there

Personal life:
1) I have it with my wife, I use it as a dropbox and he is able to pull our data whenever I need them.

2) Yesterday I was walking, and I had some ideas I wanted to note. I voiced him, but he didn't have that functionality yet. He proposed building STT (speech to text) on the VPS, and a few minutes later, it worked.

So now I also drop him voice notes and I treat him as my private assistant for journaling, insights, notes, and reminders.

I think that's my favorite use case so far.

Now I agree with Noah, asking him to build web for me is pretty painful, slow and he makes lots of mistakes. Also pages are ugly.

So instead, I SSH with Claude into my VPS and just build those websites for him. I set up SQL databases for each one and then updated OpenClaw memory.

This works much better because I keep my OpenClaw bot as a general assistant.

I use Codex, which is $20/m, and that's plenty for my use case. I don't run out of tokens, nor I have huge costs.

- stage of the project (greenfield, complex)
- framework/progamming language
- use case (i.e. building the entire app from scratch, modifying specific parts of the complex system etc.)
- tooling (for example I developed CC skills over time, memory, build tools around it, so for me it's way more efficient)
- prompting style
- level of the engineer (junior, mid, senior)

For me personally, CC wins. I gave them similar prompts and Codex implemented some ridiculous stuff. 

Also it's much easier for me to navigate CC, and I want to navigate him. Codex is much more stubborn and less flexible, but maybe that's the appeal for some. 

Codex for me is a great auditor and refactoring agent. 

And I think going forward, both will have a place in my workflow.

content:
So my non-technical friend is building an app.

He hired a dev on Fiverr.

The dev builds the app, the dashboar,d and the backend. All good, he paid, got the code. The app was ok.

He asked me to help him push it to the final stage, release it etc.

I showed him how to use Claude Code during a 3h session and for a few weeks has been hooked and he said it changed his life. He is now building a bunch of his small tools and apps that help him with everyday life.

But, back to his original app. So I spin up Claude Code and ask it to do a thorough analysis of the entire codebase to understand where we are at.

5 minutes later I get a list of issues longer that I could scroll. 

And there was also a backdoor left...

I ask Claude to examine and tell me what exactly it is.

And it turned out that the dev just left himself a backdoor endpoint triggered by a simple password (something like "pay_me") that essentially blocked the entire database. 

And you now, I can understand that it's a "security" in case someone wouldn't pay him. 

But he got paid, and still decided to give the entire codebase to my friend, including the backdoor 🫠

He could probably use it in the future, or eventually someone could find it and brute-force the password (yes, the backend had no rate limiting etc). 

My friend doesn't want to do anything with it, but I find it pretty disturbing/shocking.

content:
So recently I became less stubborn and decided to give a try to other frameworks besides Flutter for mobile apps. 

I worked with React Native, Swift and Kotlin Multiplatform. Here are my conclusions so far:

1) Indeed, native (Swift and Kotlin) looks and feels much better and "premium" almost out of the box

2) Claude Opus is doing way worse with Swift compared to Flutter or even React Native. Lots of mistakes. Lots of thread issues. 

It feels like we're back to Claude 3.5 Sonnet. I needed to do a lot of iterations to make something look or work right. Sometimes I needed to delegate it to Codex.

With Flutter... it just worked. 

3) Flutter indeed looks flat and kind of unpolished compared to native (or maybe even React Native), but it's way faster to build with it (both because Claude is good with it and also because builds are fast)

4) React Native is good and looks good, but takes a long time to build (yes yes I know Expo). Also it requires extra time on adjusting UI on both platforms so it's not as out-of-the box as Flutter.

5) KMP -- I'm still testing it and I'm still undecided whether to have one common UI or two separate. I have high hopes regarding this framework as it combines best of both worlds (native UI + cross platform logic)

So right now I'd say:
- if you go for the look and feeling, go with native or KMP or maybe with RN
- if you just build for one platform, choose native
- if you want cross-platform and you want to build it fast, have a limited budget for testing, and you don't care that much about the app "feeling", Flutter is great

Also very safe, which especially French people loved to highlight (I wonder why). Btw. I feel like 60% of the international people there are French, but I'm probably biased.

We were already thinking to organise something similar this year again. I know that many more people wanted to join, but it was too short notice for them. 

We'll see, I'm focused on building our app portfolio right now, but it would be fun.

content:
Last week I came back from Lisbon, and it was pretty epic.

The main goal was to meet up with my co-founder @ema_totaro (who is staying in Portugal for a few more months), and some other folks from the mobile space who happen to live in Lisbon.

And it was a blast.

I probably had more beers in those few days than in my entire 2025 (parents' life). 

It was nice to see real faces behind tweets and avatars that I see almost everyday. 

It also made me realise how small the mobile world is. We all knew each other and all the other in the industry. 

Not everyone was from Lisbon; some people, like @lukecarry_ (and a few others), spontaneously decided to join with just two days' notice. 

We stayed in the same hotel, so every day we had a mini breakfast, coworking/brainstorming session.

Lisbon itself is really cool. I heard so many complaints about Portugal that I had rather low expectations. It's very lively, everyone speaks English, very international, great food options, and very walkable. 

Also very safe, which especially French people loved to highlight (I wonder why). Btw. I feel like 60% of the international people there are French, but I'm probably biased.

We were already thinking to organise something similar this year again. I know that many more people wanted to join, but it was too short notice for them. 

We'll see, I'm focused on building our app portfolio right now, but it would be fun.

content:
This post brought more attention than I'd expected:)

Credits to the recent trip to Portugal (more on that later) and @jean__gatt for convincing me to try it. 

So the main reason that I think KMP/native is the way to go for me is Claude Opus. 

It changed the game, because the main selling point of cross-platform was that it was much faster to build for both platforms, but it came with the cost, which was a worst native feel, performance etc.

This week, I built a quick MVP using both native Kotlin, Swift, and Flutter. And the results were pretty clear -native looks better, duh. 

Obviously, this was a simple app, so once the complexity grows, maintaining it will be much much harder. 

That's why I want to go with KMP. One code for the logic, but separate for the UI (so a little bit more work, but still pretty fast).

Now, the issue with KMP and the reason I was delaying switching was that its support and community are still growing, so it was still easier for me to use Flutter dependencies to build fast.

BUT, this limitation kind of disappears with Claude Opus, because most of those utilities/dependencies I can just delegate to Claude and have my own custom solution if really needed. 

Things are changing fast, and we need to adapt:)

content:
Here are the pros and cons of Mallorca.

+ big expat community (20%+) so very easy to make friends, especially when you have kids, we have a big group of friends that we meet up regularly at the beach, in the park, playgrounds, by the pool etc,. It's a very outdoorsy life 

+ don't get me wrong, but there is a higher threshold to move here (higher prices, not many jobs available off-season), which means that the island attracts mostly people who managed to build their business or life outside of regular employment; so the overall "culture level" is naturally higher; if you want to move here and get a job locally, you might have a hard time 

+ great nature, great weather almost the entire year (except a few winter months) 

+ great lifestyle, laid back and happy people, safe 

+ lots to do sport-wise: biking, hiking, rock climbing, surfing, kitesurfing, windsurfing, wingfoiling, golfing, tennis, paddle, and more; the weather is very favorable for those sports

+ the island is relatively small, which makes it easy to keep in touch with everyone, even if they live on the other side of the island 

- for entrepreneurs, taxes are high and on par with those of regular employment, which I think is the biggest downside; I think that Spain would grow way faster if it were more business-friendly

- higher prices overall because it's an island; rent is also high for what you get most of the time

- to get out, you need to fly or take a ferry

- lots (and I mean LOTS) of tourists in high season

- sometimes it's harder to get or order some stuff... because it's an island

Overall, for a family life, the island is great. Easy to meet people, plenty to do, easy to move around. For single or nomads, it depends -- depends on what you like and what entertainment you prefer, for a more chill and laid-back lifestyle, I think it's also good.

We meet up with friends at least a few times a week. During summer and fall, we spend lots of time at the beach or by the pool. It's especially great with kids our age, because they just play around and we get to hang out with each other. 

I noticed that Spaniards are very sensitive when someone talks about their country in either a positive or a negative way, so I hope I won't get attacked too much for this post 🙃

content:
Since Poland is a hot topic recently, here is how the taxes in Poland look like simplified:

Sole Proprietorship:
1) "ryczałt": 2-17% flat tax + insurance (also flat, afaik ~€150-€600/m currently)
Specific taxation depends on the occupation, for example software engineer falls into the 12% bucket.
This type of taxation is low, but it doesn't allow for deducting costs.

2) "liniowy": 19% flat + insurance 4.9% flat
This type of taxation allows you to deduct costs.

3) "zasady ogólne": 12%/32%

LLC ("spółka z o.o.")
- 9% CIT below €2M 
- 19% CIT above €2M
- possible to have 0% CIT if conditions are met (employ 3 ppl etc)

Personal
- 19% capital gains tax, flat
- no gift tax between close relatives if you report it within 6 months (you need to send a simple form)

content:
ASO: screenshot AB testing for newbies

Don't have time to do it, or don't know where to start?

I managed to grow one of my apps (the one I sold) to the top positions (2-5k downloads a day at peak) in a big part thanks to changing 1st screenshot only*

I tested two things:
- text on the screenshot
- a photo

That's it.

Here is how to start simply:
1. Go to Unsplash or Nano Banana and choose or generate an image that will speak to your audience. It's like running ads; you want to get users' attention.
2. Add a big copy/title that speaks to your audience. 
3. Put it in the #1 position.
4. Release to test.
5. Wait for results
6. Based on results, go to 1. tweak photo or title (only one at the time!) and keep repeating until you convert 100% users (jk).

*It's not easy to do, and I wasn't able to repeat it for all of my apps

When we talk about ASO, everyone talks about metadata, keywords, title, screenshots, etc, but rarely anyone talks about the product side...

And I think the algo is not so stupid to just factor whether you put a keyword in the title, subtitle, or on the 2nd or 5th position in your metadata keywords.

I honestly think that there should be more focus on:
- freemium vs hard paywall 
- improving product 
- SEO (yes)

So in this screenshot, there is an app I had for almost 2y, and tbh it was pretty average, until recently I spent some time and improved it a lot.

For many months, it stayed at the 9-10 position, and now, after 1-3 weeks from the release, it suddenly jumped to #7.

Of course, it's just a singular event, so with time, we will see if the trend will continue, but it is a significant change I haven't seen in the long time. And this is what I did:
- rebuilt the website and added a lot of pages for pSEO, updated marketing url
- improved the product and I honestly think that I offer way more than my competitors
- rebuilt the onboarding slightly
- kept freemium

Personally, I think hard paywalls hurt ASO (and product metrics). I had a few apps of my own that actually dropped down when I added more aggressive upsell (but still premium though -- but I think a % of people churn just by seeing a paywall)

content:
If you're building with Flutter, this is a command that will save you a lot of time when releasing a new update.

You need to generate an API key for the App Store.

It builds the iOS release and pushes it to the App Store, then it builds the Android version and opens the folder so you can drag and drop it to Google Play.

It saved me a lot of time

flutter build ipa && xcrun altool --upload-app --type ios -f build/ios/ipa/*.ipa --apiKey your key --apiIssuer issuer id && flutter build appbundle --release && open build/app/outputs/bundle/release
